title: Estimation & Confidence Intervals
excerpt: Use a sample to estimate a population quantity, then show how uncertain that estimate is. Learn why sample size, variation and the way data are collected shape a confidence interval—and why a precise estimate can still be biased or aimed at the wrong group.
objectives: Distinguish a parameter, estimator and estimate.
Interpret standard error, bias, variance and mean squared error.
Explain the repeated-sampling meaning of a confidence interval.
Construct and communicate an interval estimate with units, assumptions and a practically meaningful comparison.
Separate sampling uncertainty from selection bias, dependence, prediction uncertainty and causal claims.

lessons.title: Name the target before calculating
lessons.body:
Start by naming the estimand: the population quantity you want, such as the average monthly excess return for a defined index and period. A parameter is that fixed population quantity. An estimator is a rule, such as the sample mean, and an estimate is the number produced by applying the rule to one sample. If 64 sampled monthly returns average 0.8%, then 0.8% per month is an estimate, not the parameter itself. Different defensible samples would give different estimates. Define the population, unit, time window, currency, return convention and sampling design first. An estimate describes a target only if the observations reasonably represent that target; a large convenience sample can be systematically off target.

A useful way to make an estimand concrete is to write a measurement statement before collecting data: “mean electricity cost per household per month, in euros, for residents of City A during January–June 2026.” Suppose a synthetic pilot records €92, €108, and €100 for three households. The sample-mean calculation is (€92 + €108 + €100) ÷ 3 = €300 ÷ 3 = €100 per household per month. Here, €100 is the estimate; the citywide six-month mean is the parameter, and “add the observations and divide by sample size” is the estimator. The result does not describe annual cost or other cities, and a volunteer sample may miss households without easy online access. For a fuller treatment, see “Penn State STAT 415 — Point Estimation” in the linked sources.

Before calculating uncertainty, decide whether each observation should represent a unit or an amount. Consider these explicitly synthetic annual borrowing rates for three firms: 4%, 6%, and 10%. If the estimand is the mean rate for a randomly selected firm, the equal-weight estimator is (4 + 6 + 10) ÷ 3 = 20 ÷ 3 = 6.67 percentage points per year (rounded). If instead the estimand is the rate paid on a randomly selected euro of borrowing, and the firms borrow €10 million, €30 million, and €60 million, the balance-weighted estimate is (4×10 + 6×30 + 10×60) ÷ (10 + 30 + 60) = 820 ÷ 100 = 8.2 percentage points per year; the euro amounts cancel because they share the same million-euro unit. Neither number is an arithmetic correction to the other: they answer different questions. State the weighting rule and target population explicitly, then assess whether firms or loan balances were measured consistently and whether the sampled firms represent the intended market. A confidence interval from the lab can describe sampling uncertainty only after that target and estimator are fixed; weighting does not remove coverage or selection bias.
lessons.takeaway: A point estimate is one result from a procedure aimed at a precisely defined population quantity.

practice.question: A study reports a sample mean fee of 1.2% for 40 sampled funds. Identify the parameter, estimator and estimate.
practice.hint: Separate the target population quantity, the rule, and the observed number.
practice.solution: The parameter is the population mean fee for the defined fund population. The estimator is the sample mean rule. The estimate is 1.2%, measured in percentage points per year if that is the stated fee unit.

lessons.title: Measure sampling variability with standard error
lessons.body:
Two samples can target the same parameter yet produce different estimates because data vary. Standard error describes the typical repeated-sample spread of an estimator. For a mean, a common estimate is SE(x̄) = s/√n, where s is the sample standard deviation in the same units as each observation and n is the number of observations. For s = 4.0 percentage points and n = 64, √n = 8, so SE = 4.0/8 = 0.5 percentage points per month. Increasing n usually narrows random sampling error at a square-root rate: quadrupling n roughly halves SE, assuming the observations and sampling design remain appropriate. Dependence, changing volatility, heavy tails or clustering can make this shortcut misleading.

Standard error is measured in the same units as the estimate, which helps distinguish it from variance. Consider a synthetic sample of 36 delivery times measured in minutes, with sample standard deviation s = 12 minutes. Since √36 = 6, the estimated standard error of the mean is 12 minutes ÷ 6 = 2 minutes. If the sample size rose to 144 while the spread stayed 12 minutes, SE would be 12 ÷ 12 = 1 minute, so four times as many observations would halve the uncertainty from 2 to 1 minute. This comparison assumes observations contribute roughly independent information and that the sample standard deviation represents the target process. It does not correct biased recruitment, clustered routes, or a changing delivery system. For a fuller treatment, see “NIST — Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals” in the linked sources.

Suppose, purely illustratively, an analyst studies monthly real sales growth for a narrowly defined market. In a synthetic sample of 49 months, the mean is 1.4% per month and the sample standard deviation is 3.5 percentage points per month. First compute √49 = 7; then SE(x̄) = 3.5 ÷ 7 = 0.50 percentage points per month. Using 1.96 as an approximate 95% critical value gives a margin of error of 1.96 × 0.50 = 0.98 percentage points, so the corresponding symmetric interval is 1.4 ± 0.98, or 0.42 to 2.38% per month. This interval describes uncertainty about the target mean under the sampling procedure; it is not a forecast for next month and does not establish that a policy caused sales growth. If the decision requires standard error no larger than 0.25 percentage points per month and the spread remains 3.5, plan n ≥ (3.5 ÷ 0.25)² = 196 months. That planning calculation assumes roughly independent observations from a stable target process; seasonality, serial dependence, or selective months could make the nominal precision too optimistic.
lessons.takeaway: Standard error measures precision under a sampling design; it does not certify that the target or sample is unbiased.

practice.question: If the standard deviation remains 6 percentage points and n increases from 25 to 100, what happens to the estimated standard error?
practice.solution: At n = 25, SE = 6/5 = 1.2 percentage points. At n = 100, SE = 6/10 = 0.6 percentage points. The sample size quadruples and the standard error halves.

lessons.title: Bias, variance and mean squared error
lessons.body:
Precision and accuracy are different. Bias is the estimator’s average deviation from the target: Bias(estimator) = E[estimator] − parameter, where E means a repeated-sampling average. Variance describes how much estimates fluctuate around their own average. Mean squared error combines both: MSE = variance + bias². Imagine two simulated estimators for the same population mean: estimator A has bias 0.0 percentage points and standard deviation 1.5 points; estimator B has bias 0.5 points and standard deviation 0.8 points. Their approximate MSEs are 2.25 and 0.89 percentage points squared, respectively. B is biased but less variable in this teaching example. More observations can reduce variance, but they do not repair survivorship, nonresponse, measurement or selection bias.

Illustrative synthetic example (January–December 2025): suppose a regional economist wants the population mean monthly electricity bill for all households, and the teaching simulation sets that target at £120 per household per month. Across repeated samples, estimator A has average error £0 and standard deviation £15, so its bias is £0 and its variance is 15² = 225 (£/month)²; its mean squared error is 225 + 0² = 225 (£/month)². Estimator B comes from a survey that under-reports bills by £5 on average, with standard deviation £8: its bias is −£5, variance is 8² = 64, and MSE is 64 + (−5)² = 89 (£/month)². B is systematically low but has lower overall squared error in this constructed comparison.

MSE can compare an estimator’s repeated-sampling performance, but it cannot establish that one estimate is correct, that the target was measured without error, or that a survey represents every household. The calculation assumes that the stated target, sampling process and error summaries are meaningful and reasonably stable over the period. Check the sampling frame against the intended household population, inspect missing or under-reported bills, and run a sensitivity analysis for plausible bias values before choosing an estimator. Do not misinterpret lower MSE as proof that an estimator is unbiased or universally best; the loss function and decision purpose matter. For the formal point-estimation framework, see “Penn State STAT 415 — Point Estimation” in the linked sources below.

The bias–variance trade-off becomes clearer when errors have the same units as the target. Imagine two synthetic estimators of mean weekly grocery spending, measured in dollars per household. Estimator A has bias $0 and standard deviation $14, so its variance is 14² = 196 dollars² and its MSE is 196 + 0² = 196 dollars². Estimator B underestimates by $3 on average and has standard deviation $8: variance = 8² = 64 dollars², and MSE = 64 + (−3)² = 73 dollars². B has lower MSE despite systematic error. This conclusion depends on the stated repeated-sampling summaries and the chosen squared-error loss; it does not prove B is best for every decision or population. For a fuller treatment, see “Penn State STAT 415 — Point Estimation” in the linked sources.

Covariance matters when estimating a change. Consider a synthetic example in which the target is the change in a monthly inflation rate, measured in percentage points. A direct paired estimator has bias +0.20 points and standard deviation 0.60 points: variance = 0.60² = 0.36 (percentage points)², so MSE = 0.36 + 0.20² = 0.40 (percentage points)². An indirect estimator subtracts separate estimates for month 1 and month 2. If their biases are +0.30 and +0.10 points, the change estimator’s bias is +0.10 − +0.30 = −0.20 points. With standard deviations 0.50 and 0.40 points and independent errors, its variance is 0.50² + 0.40² = 0.41 (percentage points)², giving MSE = 0.41 + (−0.20)² = 0.45 (percentage points)². If the errors instead have covariance 0.12 (percentage points)², the difference’s variance is 0.41 − 2(0.12) = 0.17 and its MSE is 0.17 + 0.04 = 0.21. Pairing can lower MSE by cancelling shared noise, but only when the covariance and target definition are credible; it does not cure coverage or measurement bias.
lessons.takeaway: A narrow estimate can be precisely wrong, so evaluate systematic bias as well as random spread.

practice.question: Estimator A has variance 1.44 and zero bias; estimator B has variance 0.64 and bias 0.6. Which has lower MSE?
practice.hint: Square the bias before adding it to variance.
practice.solution: A’s MSE is 1.44 + 0² = 1.44. B’s MSE is 0.64 + 0.6² = 0.64 + 0.36 = 1.00. B has the lower MSE in this example, despite its nonzero bias.

lessons.title: Build an interval from an estimate and its uncertainty
lessons.body:
A confidence interval combines a point estimate with a critical value and standard error. A common approximate form is estimate ± critical value × SE. For the illustrative monthly-return estimate 0.8%, SE 0.5 percentage points and a critical value near 2, the margin of error is 2 × 0.5 = 1.0 percentage point. The interval is 0.8% − 1.0% to 0.8% + 1.0%, or −0.2% to 1.8% per month. The critical value depends on the confidence level and reference distribution; a t procedure is often used when population spread is estimated. State whether observations are independent, how the sample was selected, and whether the approximation fits the data.

Work through the arithmetic in the units of the question. Suppose a representative sample of 100 rented homes has average weekly rent £820 and sample standard deviation £200. The estimated standard error is £200 ÷ √100 = £20. Using 1.96 as a rough 95% multiplier gives £820 ± 1.96 × £20, or about £780.80 to £859.20 per week. The interval is wider when observations vary more and narrower when the sample gives more independent information; it is not a range containing 95% of individual rents.

The coverage interpretation concerns a procedure: if we repeatedly drew suitable samples and built intervals this way, about 95% would cover the fixed population mean under the method’s assumptions. It does not mean there is a 95% probability that this already-calculated interval contains that fixed mean, and it is not a forecast of next week’s rent. Sampling uncertainty also does not automatically include nonresponse, measurement error or a poorly defined population. For formal interval construction and its assumptions, see “NIST — Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals” in the linked sources.

To construct an interval, keep the margin of error in the estimate’s units. Suppose a synthetic survey estimates average monthly transit spending at $64 per commuter, with SE = $5 and a chosen critical value of 2.1. The margin of error is 2.1 × $5 = $10.50, so the interval is $64 − $10.50 = $53.50 to $64 + $10.50 = $74.50 per commuter per month. This range describes uncertainty about the population mean under the sampling model, not the range of individual commuters’ spending. The calculation assumes the sample design and reference distribution are suitable; dependence, nonresponse, or measurement errors may widen actual uncertainty. It also does not establish what a fare change would cause. For a fuller treatment, see “NIST — Standard Errors and Confidence Intervals” in the linked sources.

A useful diagnostic is to ask whether the nominal sample size overstates independent information. Suppose, purely illustratively, a synthetic time series contains 25 quarterly observations of an inflation measure with mean 2.4% per year and sample SD 1.5 percentage points, but adjacent observations have an assumed autocorrelation of 0.40. A rough first-order design effect is (1 + 0.40)/(1 − 0.40) = 2.333, so the effective sample size is approximately 25/2.333 = 10.71 rather than 25. The independent-data SE would be 1.5/√25 = 0.30 percentage points; allowing for this dependence gives 0.30√2.333 = 0.458 percentage points. With an illustrative 95% multiplier of 2.1, the margin of error is 2.1 × 0.458 = 0.962 points, producing 2.4 − 0.962 = 1.438% to 2.4 + 0.962 = 3.362% per year, or about 1.44%–3.36%. This is still uncertainty about the average under the stated model, not a forecast or causal effect. The correction is approximate: stronger or longer-range dependence, seasonal structure, or only 25 periods may require a time-series method rather than a single design-effect adjustment.
lessons.takeaway: An interval is an estimate plus an assumption-dependent uncertainty allowance, with units that must remain visible.

practice.question: An estimate is 12 dollars, SE is 3 dollars, and the chosen critical value is 2.1. Construct the interval.
practice.hint: First calculate the margin of error, then subtract and add it.
practice.solution: Margin of error = 2.1 × 3 = 6 dollars. The interval is 12 − 6 to 12 + 6, or 6 to 18 dollars. It is conditional on the sampling and model assumptions.

lessons.title: Interpret 95% confidence without a probability mistake
lessons.body:
A 95% confidence procedure is designed so that, over many repeated samples from the same target under its assumptions, about 95% of intervals made by that procedure contain the fixed parameter. After one interval is calculated, the parameter is not randomly moving between its endpoints in the frequentist interpretation; the interval either covers it or it does not. Do not say there is a 95% probability this fixed interval contains the parameter. Instead report the estimate, interval, target population and assumptions. A historical-return interval is not a 95% chance that next month’s return lies inside it: future observations add outcome risk, and the historical sampling model may not persist.

A helpful thought experiment separates the fixed parameter from intervals that change. Suppose a synthetic process has a true mean waiting time of 10 minutes. Five repeated samples produce intervals [9.2, 10.8], [9.6, 10.4], [10.1, 11.3], [8.7, 9.9], and [9.8, 10.6] minutes. Four of these five intervals contain 10 minutes, while the fourth does not: 4 ÷ 5 = 0.80, or 80% in this tiny illustration. A 95% method would approach 95% coverage only across many repetitions, not necessarily five. The example uses a fixed target and synthetic numbers; it does not mean the current interval has a 95% probability of coverage or that future waits will lie inside it. For a fuller treatment, see “OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 7: Inference for Numerical Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)” in the linked sources.

To apply the coverage idea to a new one-sample decision, suppose—purely illustratively—that an analyst samples 36 independent, randomly selected store-months and measures monthly sales growth. The sample mean is 2.40 percentage points per month and the sample standard deviation is 3.60 percentage points per month. First compute the standard error: 3.60 pp/month ÷ √36 = 3.60 ÷ 6 = 0.60 pp/month. Because the population spread is estimated and the sample is not very large, use a t critical value of about 2.03 with 35 degrees of freedom rather than silently treating 2 as exact. The margin of error is 2.03 × 0.60 = 1.218, or about 1.22 pp/month, giving the interval 2.40 ± 1.22 = [1.18, 3.62] pp/month. A pre-specified practical benchmark of 1.00 pp/month lies below every endpoint, so the data are compatible with growth above that benchmark under the sampling assumptions. This does not predict next month’s growth or show that a policy caused sales; seasonality, clustered stores, selective measurement, and changing market conditions could invalidate the calculation. Unlike the lab’s reference display, these numbers describe a hypothetical one-sample interval.
lessons.takeaway: The 95% describes long-run coverage of the interval-making method, not a probability assigned to this fixed interval.

practice.question: Which is more accurate: ‘There is a 95% chance this interval contains the parameter’ or ‘The method covers the parameter about 95% of the time in repeated samples’? Explain.
practice.hint: Ask what is fixed and what would vary across repetitions.
practice.solution: The second statement is accurate in the frequentist framework. The parameter is fixed while the sample and interval would vary across repeated samples. The first statement assigns a probability to the already-computed interval and is not the standard confidence interpretation.

lessons.title: Read intervals for precision, importance and limits
lessons.body:
An interval supports more than a binary label. Compare it with a pre-specified practically meaningful threshold, such as a 0.5 percentage-point monthly improvement, and ask whether the plausible values would matter after fees, risk and time horizon. An interval entirely above zero may be statistically distinguishable from zero under the model, yet still be too small to matter. An interval spanning zero may reflect low precision rather than proof of no effect. Association is not prediction, and prediction is not causality: an interval around a sample mean or regression coefficient does not identify what an intervention would change. Report selection, missing data, dependence, multiple analyses and sensitivity checks. These are educational calculations, not investment advice.

Read an interval against a practical threshold, not only against zero. Suppose a synthetic evaluation estimates that a reminder lowers monthly late fees by 1.2 percentage points, with a 95% interval from 0.2 to 2.2 percentage points. If a reduction of at least 1.0 percentage point is the pre-specified meaningful threshold, the estimate exceeds it, but the interval includes values below it (0.2 and 0.8) as well as above it. Thus the data are compatible with a statistically positive but practically small reduction, or a meaningful one; more precision would help. The calculation concerns an association unless assignment and design support causality, and it does not guarantee the same effect in another population or month. For a fuller treatment, see “OpenIntro Statistics — Ch. 7: Inference for Numerical Data (CC BY-SA 3.0)” in the linked sources.

A useful planning check is to work backward from the precision you need. Suppose, purely illustratively, that monthly returns have a standard deviation of 3.0 percentage points and you want a two-sided 95% interval for the population mean with a margin of error no wider than 0.49 percentage points. Using the lab’s normal-reference calculation, set 1.96 × 3.0/√n ≤ 0.49. Rearranging gives √n ≥ 5.88/0.49 = 12, so n ≥ 144 monthly observations; at n = 144, the standard error is 3.0/12 = 0.25 percentage points and the margin is 1.96 × 0.25 = 0.49 points. If the same volatility were paired with n = 36, the standard error would be 0.50 points and the margin 0.98 points—twice as wide, not half as wide. This is a precision calculation, not evidence that 144 observations remove dependence, regime changes or selection bias. With an estimated volatility and small sample, a t critical value rather than 1.96 may be appropriate; the target population and independence assumption still require substantive justification.
lessons.takeaway: Use interval width, effect magnitude, design and consequences together; uncertainty does not disappear because a result crosses a threshold.
lessons.formula: practical comparison: interval versus a pre-specified meaningful threshold

practice.question: An estimated fee reduction is 0.3 percentage points with a 95% interval from −0.1 to 0.7 points. Can you conclude it is practically meaningful or that there is no effect?
practice.hint: Consider both the threshold and the interval’s range.
practice.solution: No. The interval includes no reduction and reductions as large as 0.7 points. It is compatible with a small or moderate effect and with no effect under the model. Compare the range with the pre-specified practical threshold and improve precision or design before making a stronger claim.

caseStudy: Consider a deliberately illustrative analyst who samples 64 monthly returns for a broad market index and obtains a mean of 0.8% per month with a sample standard deviation of 4.0 percentage points. Assuming an appropriate design and roughly independent observations, the estimated standard error is 4.0/√64 = 0.5 percentage points. Using a critical value near 2 gives a margin of error of 1.0 point and an approximate interval from −0.2% to 1.8% per month. Under repeated sampling from the same target and assumptions, a 95% interval procedure would cover the fixed population mean about 95% of the time. This does not forecast the next month, assign a 95% probability to this fixed interval, or prove that any strategy causes returns. The analyst should examine dependence, volatility regimes, period selection, missing observations, survivorship, fees, currency and whether the index defines the intended population. A practically meaningful threshold might also differ from zero. The numbers are simulated for instruction, not a historical dataset or investment recommendation.
misconceptions: There is a 95% probability that this already-computed interval contains the fixed parameter. That is not the frequentist coverage interpretation.
A smaller standard error repairs sample bias. Precision and bias are separate; a narrow interval around a selected sample can be precisely wrong.
An unbiased estimator is automatically best. Variance and mean squared error also matter, and a small bias can sometimes accompany much lower variance.
An interval containing zero proves no effect, while an interval excluding zero proves a useful or causal effect. Precision, magnitude, design and practical consequences must be considered together.
A confidence interval for a historical average is a forecast interval for the next financial outcome. Future randomness, changing regimes and model uncertainty are different sources of uncertainty.

quiz.question: What does 95% confidence mean in the repeated-sampling interpretation?
options: This fixed interval has a 95% probability of containing the parameter.
About 95% of intervals from the procedure would contain the fixed parameter under its assumptions.
95% of observations lie inside the interval.
quiz.explanation: The confidence level describes the long-run coverage of the interval-making method. It does not say that 95% of raw observations are inside the interval or assign a probability to this fixed interval.
